title: The Translation Club's Difficult Choice
passage:
A volunteer translation club at Yuto's school helped prepare English information for international visitors. At first, members believed accurate translation meant replacing each Japanese sentence with the closest English sentence possible. Their first major task was a guide to a local summer festival. The Japanese guide contained traditional terms, polite expressions, and references that local readers understood without explanation. When the club translated the text directly, the English sounded grammatical, but several exchange students found it confusing. One sentence described a portable shrine using a cultural term with no familiar English equivalent. Another politely warned visitors about entering a restricted area, but the direct translation sounded so indirect that readers did not understand it as a warning. The club debated what to do. One group wanted to preserve the original expressions as closely as possible because changing them might erase cultural meaning. Another wanted to rewrite freely so visitors could understand the practical message. Their adviser asked them to separate two kinds of accuracy: accuracy to the form of the original and accuracy to the effect the message needed to have. Neither could always be maximized at the same time. The club tested several solutions. For important cultural terms, they kept the Japanese word in Roman letters and added a short explanation the first time it appeared. For safety instructions, they used clearer and more direct English than the Japanese wording. For a historical paragraph, they kept more of the original structure because readers had time to read slowly. The students also asked exchange students to review the guide without seeing the Japanese. Their comments revealed problems the translators had missed. A sentence that seemed simple to club members used the word local in a way that made visitors wonder whether only residents were allowed to participate. Another section used the word traditional so often that it lost meaning. Yuto learned that translation was not a puzzle with one correct answer for each sentence. It required decisions about audience, purpose, context, and what information could safely be assumed. The final guide included a short note explaining that some cultural terms were left in Japanese intentionally. During the festival, volunteers observed how visitors used the guide. Most questions concerned transportation and event times rather than cultural vocabulary, so the next edition moved practical information to the front. The club's work gradually expanded from translation to communication design. They considered headings, order, maps, and the amount of explanation readers needed. Yuto came to see that faithful communication sometimes requires moving away from the surface form of the original. A warning that nobody recognizes as a warning is not successful simply because every word was translated closely. At the same time, making everything familiar to foreign readers could remove the very cultural difference the guide was meant to introduce. The club's goal became balance: preserve what matters, explain what may be unfamiliar, and make essential actions unmistakably clear.

The club later faced a harder case when translating a phrase connected with religious custom. A one-sentence English explanation could not carry every historical and emotional meaning of the original term. The students therefore placed a short practical explanation in the main guide and linked to a longer note for readers who wanted more background. Yuto realized that communication design includes not only what information to give, but also when and how much to give. Too much explanation in the main text could hide the action a visitor needed to take, while too little could make the custom seem meaningless. The club also created a decision log for difficult translations, recording the choice they made and why. New members could then understand earlier reasoning instead of starting every debate again. The record also helped reviewers distinguish deliberate choices from accidental inconsistency, which improved both quality control and confidence in later revisions. That made future editing faster and more consistent across different projects.
translation:
悠斗の学校の翻訳ボランティア部は、海外からの来訪者向け英語案内を作っていました。最初は、日本語の各文をできるだけ近い英語に置き換えることが正確な翻訳だと考えていました。しかし夏祭りの案内を直訳すると、文法は正しくても交換留学生には分かりにくい部分が多く残りました。神輿のように英語にぴったり対応する語がない文化語や、日本語では丁寧でも英語では警告だと気づきにくい立入禁止表現などです。部内では、元の表現を守るべきだという意見と、実用性を優先して自由に書き換えるべきだという意見に分かれました。顧問は、『原文の形への正確さ』と『相手に必要な効果を与える正確さ』を分けて考えるよう促しました。両方を常に最大にすることはできません。文化的に重要な語はローマ字で残し、初出時に短い説明を加える。安全案内は日本語より直接的にする。歴史説明は時間をかけて読めるため原文構造を多めに残す、といった使い分けをしました。また日本語原文を見ていない留学生に読んでもらうと、『local』の使い方から地元住民しか参加できないと誤解しそうな箇所や、『traditional』の使いすぎなど、部員が気づかなかった問題も見つかりました。悠斗は、翻訳は各文に一つの正解があるパズルではなく、読者、目的、状況、前提知識を考える作業だと学びました。祭り当日に観察すると、文化語より交通や時間の質問が多かったため、次版では実用情報を前に移しました。活動は次第に翻訳だけでなく、見出し、情報順序、地図、説明量を考えるコミュニケーション設計へ広がりました。言葉を忠実に置き換えても警告と伝わらなければ十分ではありません。一方、すべてを外国人に馴染みのある形に直せば、紹介したい文化の違いが消えてしまいます。大切なものは残し、未知のものは説明し、必要な行動は明確にする。そのバランスが部の目標になりました。

宗教的な習慣に関わる表現では、一文の英語説明だけですべての歴史的・感情的意味を伝えることはできませんでした。そこで本文には実用的な短い説明を置き、詳しく知りたい人向けの補足へつなげました。悠斗は、何を伝えるかだけでなく、いつ、どれだけ伝えるかもコミュニケーション設計の一部だと学びました。説明が多すぎれば必要な行動が埋もれ、少なすぎれば文化的意味が失われます。部では難しい翻訳判断と理由を記録するログも作り、新しい部員が過去の意図を理解できるようにしました。この記録は意図的な選択と単なる表現の揺れを区別する助けにもなり、後の編集を速く、より一貫したものにしました。
